unit.name: Paper 3: Fieldwork & UK Challenges
unit.subtitle: Geographical investigations and contemporary UK issues

lessons.title: Physical Fieldwork: Rivers & Coasts
lessons.description: Designing investigations into channel change or coastal processes using primary and secondary data.
lessons.content_html:
This lesson covers the general fieldwork skills, terminology, and exam-paper expectations that apply to every student. The specific sites, data, and methods your class actually used will be different — for the case study you’ll write about in the exam, refer to your teacher’s notes and the data you collected on the day.

Why Physical Fieldwork Matters

Physical fieldwork forces geography out of the textbook and into the field. The exam will not ask you about your trip directly, but it will give you an unfamiliar fieldwork scenario in a UK river or coastal landscape and ask you to design, carry out, present or evaluate the kind of investigation you actually did. Examiners expect you to write about your own physical investigation by name — the river, the coast, the date, the conditions — and to apply the same logic to scenarios you have never seen.

Key Fact

The six stages of the geographical enquiry process are: 1) formulate questions, 2) choose methods, 3) collect data, 4) present and process, 5) analyse and conclude, 6) evaluate.

Option 7A: River Landscapes

If your school chose a river investigation, the broad task is the same: investigate change in a river channel. A typical question is ‘How does the river channel change downstream?’ or ‘Does the river fit the Bradshaw model?’ The Bradshaw model predicts that as you move downstream, the channel widens and deepens, velocity increases, and the load becomes smaller and rounder — you test these claims at three or more sites along the river.

Edexcel requires at least one quantitative method to measure river discharge — the standard combination is width (tape measure across the channel), depth (metre rule at intervals across) and velocity (a flow meter or a floating object timed over 10 m). Discharge is then calculated as cross-sectional area × mean velocity. Edexcel also requires at least one qualitative method — usually annotated field sketches or labelled photographs that record the meanders, riffles, pools or human features at each site.

Random sampling avoids bias but can miss key features. Systematic sampling — for example a measurement every 100 m — is easy to plan but may straddle a meander or weir. Stratified sampling deliberately picks one point from each section (upper, middle, lower course) so the data represents the whole river. Most fieldwork uses systematic with a stratified element. Whatever you choose, write the reason in your method — examiners reward justified choices.

Option 7A: Coastal Landscapes

If your school chose the coast, the task is to investigate coastal processes through landscape evidence. Common questions are ‘Does longshore drift transport sediment along this beach?’ or ‘Does sediment become smaller and rounder along the beach?’ Edexcel requires one quantitative method to measure beach morphology and sediment characteristics — typically beach profiles taken with a clinometer and ranging poles, plus pebble samples measured with callipers and Powers’ roundness chart. A second quantitative option is timing oranges or table-tennis balls along the shore to measure longshore drift velocity.

The qualitative method is usually labelled field sketches of cliffs, groynes, beach huts or sea walls, or photographs annotated with arrows showing wave direction and human structures. Both methods together let you connect process (waves and current) to landform (beach shape and sediment) — exactly what the exam expects.

Risks & Practical Constraints

A risk assessment is part of the enquiry process. River fieldwork carries the risk of slippery banks, fast flows after rain and Weil’s disease from contact with rat urine in the water; coastal fieldwork carries cliff falls, rip currents, slippery rocks and tides cutting off access. Mitigations include checking river-level gauges and tide tables, working in groups, wearing wellies and gloves, and never wading above knee depth. Examiners may ask you to describe how risks were managed — vague answers (‘we were careful’) score zero; specific ones (‘we checked the Environment Agency river-level gauge that morning’) score full marks.

Secondary Data

Edexcel requires secondary data alongside your primary measurements. For rivers, that includes an Environment Agency flood risk map and one other source — for example, a hydrograph showing recent rainfall and discharge, or historical Ordnance Survey maps to show channel change. For coasts, the British Geological Survey’s online Geology of Britain viewer gives the rock type at each site and one other source might be a Shoreline Management Plan or aerial photograph of cliff retreat. Secondary data lets you set your fieldwork in a wider context — one day’s data is rarely enough on its own.

Examiners often ask ‘Justify one method used in your fieldwork.’ The trick is to link the method back to the original question. If your question is ‘Does the channel widen downstream?’, measuring channel width with a tape directly answers it — you cannot tell from a sketch alone. If your question is ‘Does sediment become rounder downstream?’, callipers and a roundness chart give numerical evidence; a photograph cannot. Always write your justification in two parts: what the method measures, and how that answers your question.

Key Fact

For physical fieldwork you must include at least one quantitative method (discharge or beach morphology), one qualitative method (sketches or annotated photographs), and at least two secondary sources. Always link methods back to the enquiry question.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When the exam shows you a fieldwork scenario you have never visited, do not panic — the skills are the same. Read the question for the command word: ‘describe’ wants what you see, ‘explain’ wants why, ‘justify’ wants pros and cons of the method, ‘evaluate’ wants a judgement. For 8-mark questions, develop two clear chains of reasoning rather than listing five undeveloped points. Always reference your own investigation by name — named rivers and coasts score better than ‘our river’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Edexcel requires one river OR coastal investigation, with one quantitative method, one qualitative method and at least two secondary sources.
  • River fieldwork measures discharge and channel change; coastal fieldwork measures beach morphology, sediment and longshore drift.
  • Sampling, risk assessment and method justification all link back to the original enquiry question and earn marks when you make that link explicit.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a quantitative method of recording channel change in a river investigation?
A) Annotated field sketch
B) Photograph of meanders
C) Tape measure of channel width
D) Verbal description by a resident
practice_questions.marks: C) Tape measure of channel width [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two pieces of secondary data that could be used in a coastal landscape investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each (max 2). Examples:
• A British Geological Survey geology map showing rock type along the coast
• A Shoreline Management Plan describing planned coastal management
• An aerial photograph showing cliff retreat over time
• Tide tables
• Wave-rider buoy data on wave height and direction
[Max 2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason for using systematic sampling in a river fieldwork investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for a developed reason.
Example: Systematic sampling means measurements are taken at fixed intervals along the river (1) which makes it easy to plan and ensures sites are evenly spread from upper to lower course (1), so changes in width, depth and velocity downstream can be compared fairly (1).
Alternative: speed of data collection in limited fieldwork time. [Max 3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A student timed an orange floating along 10 m of beach water in 22 seconds. Calculate the longshore drift velocity in metres per second, giving your answer to one decimal place. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 1 for correct formula, 2 for working, 1 for answer with units.
Formula: velocity = distance ÷ time = 10 ÷ 22 (1)
Working: 10 ÷ 22 = 0.4545... (1) (1 for correct calculation)
Answer: 0.5 m/s to 1 decimal place (1) [-1 if no units]
[Max 4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a student could plan a coastal fieldwork investigation to test whether sediment becomes rounder along a beach. Refer to methods, sampling and risks.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 6 marks: 1–2 = simple list; 3–4 = some development; 5–6 = developed methods linked to question with sampling and risk addressed.
Indicative content:
• Stratified sampling along beach (e.g. 5 sites at 100 m spacing) so data represents whole stretch (1+1)
• At each site, randomly pick 10 pebbles, measure roundness using Powers' roundness chart and size with callipers (1+1)
• Annotated photographs at each site as qualitative evidence of pebble shape (1)
• Risk assessment: tide times checked, gloves worn, never sample alone (1)
• Compare mean roundness scores between sites to test whether pebbles round in the direction of longshore drift (1)
[Max 6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the methods you used in your physical fieldwork investigation. In your answer you should:
• name your investigation and its question
• describe two methods you used
• explain strengths and weaknesses of each
• reach a justified conclusion about the reliability of your data.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained, well-evidenced evaluation. Names a specific investigation and question, describes two methods accurately, develops both strengths and weaknesses for each, reaches a justified judgement about reliability.
Secure (5–6): Clear evaluation. Names investigation, describes two methods; some strengths and weaknesses; conclusion present but partially justified.
Developing (3–4): Some evaluation. Investigation named, methods described in general terms; mostly one-sided; no clear conclusion.
Emerging (1–2): Simple description of methods. Limited evaluation. No investigation named.
Indicative content (river example): Strengths of width/depth measurement = simple, repeatable, gives clear data. Weaknesses = one day's snapshot, weather may not be typical, equipment error. Strength of sketches = qualitative context. Weaknesses = subjective. Conclusion should weigh whether two methods together gave a reliable answer.

lessons.title: Human Fieldwork: Urban & Rural Settlements
lessons.description: Investigating change in city centres or rural settlements using quantitative and qualitative methods.
lessons.content_html:
This lesson covers the general fieldwork skills, terminology, and exam-paper expectations that apply to every student. The specific sites, data, and methods your class actually used will be different — for the case study you’ll write about in the exam, refer to your teacher’s notes and the data you collected on the day.

Two Choices, Same Skill Set

Edexcel asks every student to carry out a second investigation in a human environment. You either looked at change in a central or inner urban area — the kind of place that shifts from week to week as shops close, flats are built and footfall changes — or you looked at change in rural settlements, where the question is more about counter-urbanisation, second homes, or thinning bus services. The skills are the same: ask a focused question, choose appropriate methods, collect data fairly, present and analyse it, then reflect on what went wrong.

Key Fact

For human fieldwork Edexcel requires at least one quantitative method, one qualitative method and at least two secondary sources, including Census data from the Office for National Statistics.

Option 7B: Central or Inner Urban Areas

A typical urban question is ‘How is the central business district changing?’ or ‘How does environmental quality vary across the inner urban area?’ Two methods cover the brief.

First, a quantitative land-use survey: walking each street and ticking off whether a building is comparison retail (e.g. clothes), convenience retail (e.g. supermarket), services (e.g. hairdresser), leisure or vacant. Compared with old maps or business directories, this shows how the area has changed — for example, the rise of independent coffee shops or the loss of department stores. Second, a qualitative environmental quality survey (EQS), where the same set of scores (1–5) is recorded at sample sites — usually for litter, noise, graffiti, building condition and green space. Bipolar scales (e.g. clean ↔ dirty) reduce, but do not remove, observer bias.

Subjective judgement is the EQS’s big weakness: one student scores rust on a railing as a 2, another scores it as a 4. Three fixes work in practice. Calibration — the whole class scores one site together before splitting up, agreeing what a 3 looks like. Triple sampling — three students score the same site and the mean is taken. Photo logging — every score is paired with a photograph so judgements can be re-checked later. Examiners reward students who name a fix, not just complain about bias.

Option 7B: Rural Settlements

If your school chose a rural settlement, the broad task is to investigate change. A typical question is ‘How is village A changing because of counter-urbanisation?’ Edexcel requires one quantitative method to measure flows of people within the settlement — usually pedestrian counts at four or five points (junctions, the bus stop, the village shop) for a fixed period (e.g. 10 minutes), repeated at different times of day. Counts can be displayed on flow lines on a map of the village.

The required qualitative method records the views of people on the quality of the rural environment — typically a questionnaire with both closed (tick-box) and open (free-text) questions, or recorded interviews with residents, second-home owners and shopkeepers. Open responses give context that numbers cannot — one resident’s comment that ‘the new estate killed the village pub’ tells you more about change than a footfall figure.

Sampling Real People

Sampling matters even more in human fieldwork because people are far less uniform than rocks. Random sampling means stopping every fifth passer-by; systematic sampling means standing at fixed sites; stratified sampling deliberately balances ages, genders and tourists vs locals so the sample reflects the village as a whole. Sample size matters too: 50 questionnaires give a much more reliable picture than 10. The exam often shows you a small sample and asks how reliability could be improved — the obvious answers are ‘more questionnaires’ and ‘sample on different days/times’.

Required Secondary Sources

For both options Edexcel requires Census data from the ONS as one secondary source. The Census is taken every 10 years (most recently in 2021) and gives age structure, ethnicity, occupation, housing tenure and tens of other variables for every tiny output area. The second source can be chosen by the school: an old map showing land use 50 years ago; ONS Neighbourhood Statistics for a rural parish; police crime data; or estate agent data on house prices. Always state the source and date in the analysis.

Stopping members of the public requires care. Approach in pairs, in a public place, in daylight; introduce yourself, give a name and the school; explain the survey is anonymous; never ask under-16s without an adult present. People can refuse, and you must record refusals as a non-response — it affects sample size. Photographing people, especially children, is not allowed without permission. These rules protect both you and your respondents, and a strong evaluation will mention them.

Key Fact

Reliability of EQS scores improves through calibration before fieldwork, triple-sampling at each site, photo logging, and increasing sample size. Naming a specific fix in the exam scores higher than complaining about bias.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Human fieldwork questions often look at sample size and bias. If the exam asks ‘Suggest one way the student could improve their data,’ never say ‘ask more people’ alone — develop it: ‘Increase the sample to at least 50 respondents and split them across weekday/weekend so the data is not biased to commuters or shoppers.’ The 8-mark questions reward chains of reasoning, so develop two clear improvements rather than listing six undeveloped ones.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • For urban areas, a land-use survey (quantitative) and environmental quality survey (qualitative) measure change in central or inner districts.
  • For rural settlements, pedestrian counts (quantitative) and questionnaires or interviews (qualitative) capture flows and resident views.
  • All human fieldwork must use ONS Census data plus one other secondary source, manage ethical risks and use sampling that reflects the community.

practice_questions.text:
Which method is best described as quantitative human fieldwork?
A) Open-ended interview with the village postmaster
B) Pedestrian count of footfall at four points
C) Annotated photograph of a high street
D) Sketch of a vacant shop window
practice_questions.marks: B) Pedestrian count of footfall at four points [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why questionnaires are useful in rural fieldwork.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each (max 2). Examples:
• They collect the views of residents that numbers alone miss.
• They allow comparison across age groups and length of residence.
• Closed questions give quantitative data; open questions give qualitative context.
• They can be repeated and standardised across investigators.
[Max 2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way an environmental quality survey can be made more reliable.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for a developed point.
Example: Calibrating scores before fieldwork (1) by having the whole class score one site together and agree what a 3 looks like (1) reduces variation between observers, so the data from different teams is comparable (1).
Alternative: triple sampling at each site, photo logging, increasing sample size, repeating at different times of day. [Max 3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A student counted 96 pedestrians in 12 minutes at a village high street. Calculate the mean rate of pedestrians per minute and per hour. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 1 for correct working per minute, 1 for value, 1 for working per hour, 1 for value with units.
Working: 96 ÷ 12 = 8 (1) per minute (1)
Working: 8 × 60 = 480 (1) per hour (1) [-1 if no units]
Alternative correct route: 96 × 5 = 480 per hour (60/12 = 5).
[Max 4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a student could plan a fieldwork investigation into change in a UK city centre. Refer to methods, sampling and a secondary data source.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 6 marks: 1–2 = simple list; 3–4 = some development; 5–6 = developed methods linked to question with sampling and secondary source.
Indicative content:
• Land-use survey along a transect from the railway station to the inner ring road, recording each property as retail, services or vacant (1+1)
• Environmental quality survey at five sites scored on litter, graffiti, noise (1)
• Stratified sampling so sites cover both prime retail core and edge of CBD (1)
• Compare with ONS Census 2011 vs 2021 to show population and ethnicity change (1)
• Use a historic Goad map to show how shop occupancy has changed (1)
[Max 6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the reliability of the data you collected in your human fieldwork investigation. In your answer you should:
• name the investigation and its question
• describe two methods you used
• explain factors that may have reduced reliability
• reach a justified conclusion about how reliable the data was overall.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained, well-evidenced evaluation. Names a specific investigation and question, describes two methods, develops at least two reliability factors (e.g. sample size, observer bias, time of day, weather), reaches a justified judgement.
Secure (5–6): Clear evaluation. Investigation named with two methods; some reliability factors; conclusion present but partially justified.
Developing (3–4): Some evaluation. Investigation named, methods described in general terms; mostly one-sided; no clear conclusion.
Emerging (1–2): Simple description of methods. Limited evaluation. No investigation named.
Indicative content (urban example): Strengths = repeatable land-use categories, ONS data covers whole city. Weaknesses = small EQS sample, only one weekday, observer bias on subjective scores. Conclusion should weigh whether reliability is good enough to justify the conclusions drawn.

glossary_terms.definition: A survey that records what each shop, office or building is used for, classified into categories such as comparison retail, convenience retail, services and vacancy.
A scoring sheet used to record subjective judgements about a place, such as litter, noise or graffiti, on a scale of 1 to 5.
Sampling that deliberately includes a balance of different age, gender or ethnic groups so the sample reflects the whole community.

lessons.title: Presenting & Analysing Fieldwork Data
lessons.description: Choosing graphs and maps to display fieldwork findings, and writing conclusions that link to the question.
lessons.content_html:
This lesson covers the general fieldwork skills, terminology, and exam-paper expectations that apply to every student. The specific sites, data, and methods your class actually used will be different — for the case study you’ll write about in the exam, refer to your teacher’s notes and the data you collected on the day.

Why Presentation Matters

Raw fieldwork data is just numbers and notes. To answer a geographical question you need to present it in a form that lets you see patterns — and the form has to fit the data. Choosing the wrong graph or map throws marks away. The exam often shows you data in a table or graph and asks you to describe a trend, calculate a statistic, or pick a better way of presenting it. The same logic applies to your own investigation: every piece of data you collected should appear in your write-up in the form most suited to its type.

Key Fact

Match the graph to the data: line graphs for continuous change, bar charts for categories, pie charts for percentages of a total, scatter graphs for paired variables, and flow lines or choropleth maps for spatial data.

Common Graph Choices

A line graph shows continuous change — river velocity at sites 1–5 along a course, or pedestrian count over the day. A bar chart compares categories — types of land use in a CBD, or visitor age groups in a National Park. A pie chart shows shares of a whole — the proportion of vacant vs occupied shops — but only when categories add to 100%. A scatter graph tests a relationship between two variables — pebble size against distance downstream. A compound (stacked) bar shows two layers at once, e.g. occupied vs vacant shops at five sites.

Maps for Spatial Data

Maps are essential when location matters. A choropleth map shades areas by value — perfect for population density across a city or footfall categories across village zones. A flow-line map uses thick arrows to show movement — ideal for showing pedestrian flows along high streets, or river discharge at survey points. Proportional symbols place a circle or square at each site, sized to match the value — for example, footfall counts at five village locations.

Edexcel asks you to be comfortable with both hand-drawn and computer-generated presentation. GIS tools like Esri ArcGIS Online or Digimap let you layer data onto base maps quickly, calculate buffer zones around features and analyse spatial patterns. Hand-drawn maps stay essential because the exam expects you to be able to interpret and complete maps and graphs by hand. Skills examiners look for include adding a title, scale bar, north arrow, key, and accurate labelling. Marks are lost for missing units on a graph axis or no key on a choropleth.

Describing & Analysing Patterns

When the exam says ‘describe the pattern shown,’ you must do three things: state the overall trend, quote specific figures from the data, and identify any anomalies — sites or values that go against the pattern. Examiners use the formula TEA: Trend, Examples, Anomalies. So instead of writing ‘footfall increases from morning to lunchtime,’ write ‘footfall rose from 32/min at 9 a.m. to a peak of 78/min at 12:30, before falling to 41/min at 4 p.m.; site 4 was an anomaly with only 12/min, possibly because it lay on a back street.’

Statistical Tools

Edexcel expects you to be able to calculate basic statistics. The median is a useful average for skewed data such as pebble size, where one boulder can pull the mean. The interquartile range shows how spread out the data is. Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100; this often appears in change-over-time questions. Always show your working in the exam — calculations marks are easy to lose by missing units or not rounding clearly.

Conclusions That Answer the Question

A conclusion is not a description — it is a direct answer to the original enquiry question, supported by your own data and any wider geographical theory. The structure that scores well is: (1) restate the question, (2) state your overall finding, (3) quote two pieces of evidence, (4) link to a relevant model or case study, (5) acknowledge the most important limitation. For example: ‘Our investigation asked whether the river fits the Bradshaw model. Site 5 had three times the discharge of site 1, and pebble roundness rose from 1.2 to 3.4. This broadly supports the model, although the steep, narrow channel at site 3 was an anomaly — perhaps because of a recently engineered weir.’

Stage 6 of the enquiry process is reflection: critically reviewing methods, data and conclusions. Examiners distinguish between describing (what happened) and evaluating (whether it was reliable). A strong evaluation names a specific weakness (small sample, weather on the day, observer bias) and explains how it affected the result, then suggests a realistic improvement. Vague comments (‘the data was not very reliable’) score nothing without a reason and a fix.

Key Fact

For describing data, use TEA: Trend, Examples (two figures), Anomalies. For conclusions, restate the question, give your finding, support with two pieces of evidence and end with one acknowledged limitation.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Calculation marks are the easiest marks on the paper to lose — show working line by line, double-check units (m/s, %, m3), and round only at the final step. For describe questions, examiners watch for at least two pieces of data and one anomaly — if you don’t reference figures, the maximum is half marks. For conclusion or evaluation questions, always tie your answer back to the original investigation question rather than just summarising your data.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pick the graph for the data: line for continuous change, bar for categories, pie for shares, scatter for relationships, flow lines or choropleth for spatial patterns.
  • Describe data using the TEA structure — trend, examples with figures, anomalies — and back conclusions with named evidence.
  • Reflection is the sixth stage of the enquiry process: name a specific weakness, explain its effect, and suggest a realistic improvement.

practice_questions.text:
Which presentation method best displays the proportion of land use categories in a city centre?
A) Line graph
B) Pie chart
C) Scatter graph
D) Climograph
practice_questions.marks: B) Pie chart [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:

Developing (3–4): Some evaluation. Investigation named, conclusion stated; limitations limited; no clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2): Simple description of conclusion only. No specific limitations or judgement.
Indicative content (river example): Conclusion supported because discharge tripled along course, pebbles rounded; limitation = single day, anomaly at site 3 not fully explained, sample size small. Judgement should weigh whether the conclusion is justified given those limits.

lessons.title: UK Resources & Sustainability Challenge
lessons.description: How a growing UK population stresses ecosystems and resources, plus sustainable transport responses.
lessons.content_html:
A Country Under Pressure

The UK’s population reached around 68 million in 2025 and is forecast to pass 73 million by 2050, driven mainly by net migration of around 300,000 a year and slowly rising life expectancy. Each extra person needs food, water, energy, housing and transport — and that adds up fast on an island the size of Britain. Geographers ask three connected questions about this challenge: how is consumption changing, how is the environment coping, and how can we live better without exhausting what is left?

Key Fact

The UK population is projected to grow from around 68 million in 2025 to 73 million by 2050. Each extra person consumes about 500 m3 of water and 4–5 tonnes of CO2 per year, raising pressure on water supply, food production and the climate.

Changing Consumption Patterns

Population is only half the story. Per-person consumption is also shifting. The average UK home in 2025 contains over 30 electrical devices, more than double the figure 25 years ago. Online shopping has multiplied delivery van traffic and packaging waste — carbon footprint calculations show UK households throw away around 100 kg of plastic each year. Diets, however, have become slightly less meat-heavy than in the 2000s, and electricity use per home has fallen due to LED lighting and efficient appliances. The picture is mixed: some pressures are easing, others are intensifying.

Pressure on UK Ecosystems

UK ecosystems face several growing pressures. Habitat loss from new housing has fragmented hedgerows and wetlands — the State of Nature 2023 report found that 1 in 6 UK species is now at risk of extinction. Air and water pollution: only 14% of English rivers reach ‘good ecological status’ under the Water Framework Directive, harmed by farm fertiliser run-off and untreated sewage. Climate change is shifting species ranges; insects such as the Essex skipper butterfly are spreading north faster than birds can adapt. Tourism pressure on National Parks erodes footpaths and disturbs wildlife.

The Lake District welcomes around 18 million visitors a year, generating £1.4 billion of tourism income. But footpaths erode at popular peaks like Helvellyn (the National Trust spent £1.5 million repairing paths in the 2010s). Lake water quality declines as boats churn sediment and run-off from farms enters tributaries. Second-home ownership pushes house prices beyond local wages — in 2023 the average Lake District home cost 11.6 times average local earnings. The Park Authority responds with footpath repair, sustainable farming grants under Environmental Land Management schemes, and limits on second-home conversions in some parishes.

Sustainable Transport: National Options

Transport produces about 27% of UK carbon emissions, with cars and vans alone responsible for over half of that. Sustainable transport aims to reduce that footprint while still moving people and freight. The UK government’s 2030 ban on new petrol and diesel car sales pushes drivers toward electric vehicles — over 30% of new car sales were electric in 2024. Rail electrification, including the Great Western route to Cardiff, replaces diesel locomotives. Active travel — walking and cycling — is being invested in through schemes like the £200 million National Cycle Network expansion. Bus franchising in Greater Manchester (Bee Network, 2024) gives the mayor power to set routes and fares, encouraging modal shift away from cars.

Tensions in the Sustainable Transport Plan

Sustainable transport sounds neat but creates genuine conflict. EVs cut tailpipe emissions but their batteries need lithium and cobalt mined elsewhere — sometimes with severe local impacts. HS2, originally a flagship sustainable rail project, was scaled back in 2023 to a London-Birmingham line, leaving northern England feeling short-changed. Cycle lanes shrink road space for cars and have triggered fierce local opposition (e.g. London’s Low Traffic Neighbourhoods). Rural areas, where over 90% of journeys are by car, find it hard to switch — bus services have fallen by a third since 2010 outside cities.

National policy alone is not enough. Bottom-up schemes — community energy projects, town-scale 20 mph zones, lift-share apps — cut emissions while bringing residents on board. Bristol’s Clean Air Zone (2022) charges higher-polluting vehicles £9 to enter the city centre, and revenue funds local cycling. The combination of top-down rules (zero-emission deadlines, electrification) with local action (bike hire, car-free streets, EV charging in supermarket car parks) is what makes sustainability politically possible. The exam will reward students who can name both scales.

Key Fact

Sustainable UK transport options include electric vehicles, rail electrification, active travel infrastructure and bus franchising. Each cuts emissions but creates new conflicts — mining for batteries, lost road space, or unequal benefits between cities and rural areas.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 8-mark synoptic questions on UK challenges, examiners want links to other parts of the spec — population (Topic 4), ecosystems (Topic 3) and resources (Topic 6) all feed in. Aim to name two specific UK examples (e.g. Lake District tourism, Manchester Bee Network) and contrast them. Avoid vague answers about ‘the environment’ — specific places, figures and dates score the higher bands.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • UK population growth and rising consumption put pressure on water, food, energy and ecosystems — only 14% of English rivers reach good ecological status.
  • Tourism pressures National Parks (Lake District footpaths and second-home prices); planning and farming reforms try to manage this without removing access.
  • Sustainable transport relies on a mix of electrification, rail, active travel and franchising — but each option creates winners, losers and rural/urban tensions.

lessons.title: UK Settlement, Population & Economic Challenge
lessons.description: The UK two-speed economy, brownfield versus greenfield, and migration debates that shape settlement.
lessons.content_html:
The Two-Speed Economy

For more than 30 years the UK has had a two-speed economy: London and the South East grow much faster than the rest of the UK. London alone produces around 22% of UK economic output despite being home to only 13% of the population. By contrast, regions such as the North East, Wales and parts of Northern Ireland have GDP per head only 60–70% of the UK average. Wage gaps follow the same line: median weekly earnings in London were £853 in 2023, against £629 in the North East — a gap of more than £200 a week.

Key Fact

London produces around 22% of UK output with 13% of the population. Median weekly pay in London (£853, 2023) is over £200 above the North East (£629), and house prices average around 11× earnings in London versus 5× in the north.

Bridging the Gap

UK governments have tried several strategies to narrow the divide. The Northern Powerhouse, launched in 2014, aimed to link Manchester, Leeds, Liverpool, Sheffield and Newcastle into a single ‘super-region’ through better transport (HS2 phase 2 was originally part of this) and devolution of budgets to mayors. The Levelling Up Fund, announced in 2020, has poured around £4.8 billion into local regeneration projects since 2021 — new museums, station upgrades, school refurbishments. Freeports at Teesside, Liverpool, Plymouth and elsewhere offer tax breaks to attract manufacturing. Critics argue results are patchy: HS2 was scaled back in 2023 to a London-Birmingham line, the productivity gap with London barely budged through the 2010s, and money is often spread thinly across small projects.

Brownfield vs Greenfield

Wherever the UK builds, the same argument repeats. Brownfield sites — ex-factories, old gas works, derelict warehouses — sit close to existing infrastructure, jobs and shops. Building on them protects the countryside and cuts car use. London’s Olympic Park (built on contaminated industrial land in Stratford) and Manchester’s Salford Quays (the old docks) are textbook brownfield successes. Drawbacks include high costs to clean contaminated soil and complex demolition.

Greenfield sites are cheaper, easier and quicker to build on. Most large-scale housing estates in the UK — e.g. on the edge of Cambridge, York or Milton Keynes — sit on what used to be fields. The drawback is irreversible loss of countryside, increased car dependency, and pressure on water and drainage. The Campaign to Protect Rural England estimates 290,000 homes are planned on Green Belt land by 2026.

Salford Quays shows the brownfield model at full scale. From the 1980s, ITV, the BBC, hotels, restaurants and over 8,000 new homes turned the derelict Manchester Ship Canal docks into a working media district. Jobs grew from near-zero in 1985 to over 17,000 by 2018. But locals point out new flats are unaffordable to long-time residents, and tower blocks now dominate skylines that were industrial. Green-field equivalents do not face this gentrification pressure but consume open land. The exam often asks ‘which is better?’ — a strong answer says ‘it depends on context’ and gives one example each.

Migration: The Numbers

Net migration to the UK was around 685,000 in 2023 (the latest full year), a record level driven partly by Ukrainian and Hong Kong resettlement schemes, partly by international students, and partly by NHS and care worker visas. The Office for National Statistics revises these figures — a 2024 update raised earlier estimates by around 100,000 — reminding us that migration data is uncertain. Large UK cities (especially London, Birmingham, Manchester) absorb most arrivals, although smaller cities such as Boston in Lincolnshire and Peterborough have seen the biggest percentage changes in their populations.

Stakeholder Views on Migration

Stakeholders differ sharply. Business groups argue migration fills shortages in care homes, agriculture and IT — British farmers have warned that crops have been left unpicked since seasonal worker visas were tightened. The NHS relies on overseas doctors and nurses for around 17% of its workforce. Concerned residents point to pressure on housing, school places and GP appointments — especially in towns where housing supply has not kept up. Government tries to balance these by adjusting the points-based visa system — raising the minimum salary to £38,700 in 2024, which cut some migration but worsened care-sector shortages.

UK migration figures rely on several overlapping sources: the International Passenger Survey, Home Office visa data, NHS GP registrations and the Census. The IPS sample was tiny — around 700,000 passengers a year — and was suspended in 2020 due to COVID, so 2020–22 estimates are particularly uncertain. The ONS now uses Home Office and HMRC administrative data instead, which is more accurate for non-EU arrivals but slower to release. Always treat any single migration headline with caution — figures are routinely revised, and the political debate often gets ahead of the data.

Key Fact

UK net migration was around 685,000 in 2023. Stakeholders disagree: business and the NHS argue it fills skills gaps, residents point to housing and service pressure, and government tries to balance the two through visa rules.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Synoptic 8-mark questions often combine settlement, population and economic challenges. Examiners reward candidates who can link two parts of the spec — for example, brownfield development as a response to population growth, or migration as a driver of urban regeneration. Always include figures (London’s share of GDP, net migration totals, Levelling Up budget) and reach a clear judgement, not a fence-sitting summary.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The UK two-speed economy persists despite Northern Powerhouse, Levelling Up and Freeports — London still leads on output, wages and house prices.
  • Brownfield (Salford Quays, Olympic Park) protects countryside but costs more and risks gentrification; greenfield is cheaper but loses countryside permanently.
  • UK net migration of around 685,000 in 2023 fills skills gaps but pressures local services; stakeholders read the same numbers very differently.

lessons.title: UK Landscape & Climate Change Challenge
lessons.description: National Parks, flood management and how a warming climate is reshaping the UK landscape.
lessons.content_html:
Landscapes Under Pressure

The UK’s most distinctive landscapes — the Lake District, the Pembrokeshire coast, the Cairngorms, Snowdonia — are not wilderness. They are National Parks: 15 in the UK, covering around 8% of the country, where the public authority must conserve the landscape and ecology while keeping it open for visitors. Pressures are growing on every front. Climate change is shifting weather, vegetation and erosion rates. Flood risk is rising along rivers and coasts. Visitor numbers and second-home demand strain housing and infrastructure. Topic 8 expects you to weigh up these pressures and the management responses.

Key Fact

The UK’s 15 National Parks have two statutory purposes — conserve and enhance natural beauty and wildlife, and promote understanding and enjoyment by the public. Where these conflict, conservation takes priority (the ‘Sandford Principle’).

Conservation vs Development

Park authorities must constantly balance two pressures: keeping the landscape recognisable and supporting the people who live in it. In the Lake District, second-home conversions push average house prices to over 11× local earnings, so young workers leave; planning rules now restrict new homes to local-occupancy in some parishes. In Snowdonia, hydropower schemes generate clean energy but cut tracks across mountainsides, splitting opinion among walkers and conservationists. The Yorkshire Dales has used Environmental Land Management payments to pay farmers to restore peat bogs — a win for carbon storage and flood control, although it changes how some valleys look.

Flood Risk: Rivers & Coasts

Flood risk is rising for two reasons. First, climate change brings more intense rainfall — the UK saw record February 2020 floods after Storms Ciara, Dennis and Jorge dumped 200–300 mm of rain in two weeks. Second, urban growth has paved over fields that used to soak up water. Around 5.7 million UK properties are at flood risk, and the Environment Agency expects this to rise.

Hard engineering uses concrete to hold back water — the Thames Barrier (closed over 220 times since 1982), Boscastle’s harbour wall, sea walls along the Yorkshire and East Anglian coasts. Hard defences work, but they are expensive, age fast and shift the problem along the coast. Soft engineering works with natural processes — tree planting in upper catchments, restoring meanders straightened decades ago, beach nourishment with imported sand, and managed realignment that lets the sea reclaim low-value farmland to absorb storm surges. The 2014 Medmerry managed-realignment scheme on the West Sussex coast removed 7 km of crumbling sea wall and let the tide return, creating wetlands that buffer Selsey behind it.

In Pickering, North Yorkshire, the ‘Slowing the Flow’ scheme spent around £3.2 million from 2010 to plant 40,000 trees in upland catchments, build 167 small ‘leaky dams’ from logs and create a flood storage reservoir. The combination slowed run-off so peak river flow into Pickering town centre dropped by an estimated 15–20%. The town flooded in 1999, 2000, 2002 and 2007 — but stayed dry through Storm Desmond in 2015 when neighbouring towns flooded badly. Costs are far lower than concrete defences and the scheme also boosts wildlife and carbon storage.

UK Climate Change — What’s Already Changing

UK climate is already shifting. Met Office records show annual mean temperature rose by about 1.0°C between 1981–2010 and 2014–2023. Summers are getting hotter (July 2022 hit 40.3°C at Coningsby in Lincolnshire — the first time the UK passed 40°C). Winters are warmer and wetter; snowfall in the Cairngorms ski resorts has shortened the season by around 30 days since the 1980s. Sea levels around the UK have risen by around 18 cm since 1900 and continue to rise. Flooding from intense rainfall is now Britain’s most common climate hazard.

Future Uncertainty

How much more change comes depends on global emissions. The Met Office’s UK Climate Projections (UKCP18) sketch out a low-, medium- and high-emissions future. By the 2070s, summers could be 3–5°C hotter under high emissions, and winters 25% wetter. Sea level around London could rise 0.7–1.0 m. But uncertainty is genuine: how the UK’s climate behaves also depends on the position of the jet stream, ocean circulation in the North Atlantic, and on land-use changes that affect how much water soaks in. Predictions narrow as emissions paths become clearer.

National responses focus on mitigation — the legally binding 2050 Net Zero target, offshore wind expansion (the UK now generates over 40% of its electricity from renewables), and the 2030 ban on new petrol and diesel cars. Local adaptation includes installing larger drains, raising flood defences, planting urban trees to cool city centres (London’s ‘Cool Streets’), and grants to households for sustainable drainage. The Climate Change Committee’s 2024 progress report warned the UK is on track to miss its 2030 emissions target, so policy may tighten further in the late 2020s.

Key Fact

Mitigation cuts emissions (UK 2050 Net Zero, >40% renewable electricity); adaptation copes with impacts already happening (Pickering Slowing the Flow, Medmerry managed realignment, urban tree planting). Effective policy needs both at the same time.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The 12-mark evaluation is the heaviest question on this paper. Examiners want both sides plus a justified judgement. For climate or flood-management questions, name two specific UK examples (e.g. Pickering Slowing the Flow vs Thames Barrier), explain how each works, weigh costs against benefits, and end with a clear conclusion — not a fence-sitting summary. Spelling, punctuation and grammar count for an extra 4 marks on this paper, so reread before moving on.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • UK National Parks balance conservation with public access and the needs of residents — conflicts include second homes, hydropower and farming reform.
  • Hard flood defences (Thames Barrier) protect cities at high cost; soft schemes (Pickering, Medmerry) work with natural processes and bring co-benefits.
  • UK climate has already warmed by around 1°C; future change is uncertain but likely brings hotter summers, wetter winters and rising seas — needing both mitigation and adaptation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of soft engineering for UK flood management?
A) Thames Barrier in London
B) Concrete sea wall along the Yorkshire coast
C) Tree planting and 'leaky dams' upstream of Pickering
D) Tidal lock gates at the Boston Barrier
practice_questions.marks: C) Tree planting and 'leaky dams' upstream of Pickering [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two impacts of climate change already observed in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each (max 2). Examples:
• Annual mean temperature has risen by around 1.0 °C in recent decades
• July 2022 was the first UK day above 40 °C (40.3 °C at Coningsby)
• Sea level around the UK has risen by about 18 cm since 1900
• Cairngorms ski season has shortened by around 30 days
• Floods from intense rainfall have become more frequent
[Max 2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage of soft engineering for UK flood management.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for a developed advantage.
Example: Soft engineering, such as tree planting in upper catchments (1), slows the rate at which rainwater reaches the river (1), reducing peak discharge so towns downstream are less likely to flood (1).
Alternative: Cheaper than concrete; ecological co-benefits (carbon, biodiversity); creates leisure spaces. [Max 3 marks]

practice_questions.text: The Pickering 'Slowing the Flow' scheme cost £3.2 million and reduced peak flow by 17% in storm conditions. Calculate the cost of reducing each 1% of peak flow, to the nearest thousand pounds.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 1 for method, 1 for working, 1 for value, 1 for rounding/units.
Method: divide £3,200,000 by 17 (1)
Working: 3,200,000 ÷ 17 = 188,235.29 (1+1)
Answer: £188,000 to nearest thousand pounds (1)
[Max 4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how managing a UK National Park causes conflict between different stakeholders.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 6 marks: 1–2 = simple list; 3–4 = some development; 5–6 = developed conflicts with named stakeholders and figures.
Indicative content (Lake District):
• Tourists want access to honeypots like Helvellyn (1) but eroded paths cost £1.5 million to repair (1)
• Local residents face house prices 11.6× earnings due to second homes (1) so young people leave (1)
• Farmers want subsidies for grazing while conservation groups want rewilding and peat bog restoration (1+1)
• Park authority must balance the Sandford Principle: conservation prioritised when in genuine conflict (1)
[Max 6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate whether UK responses to climate change focus too much on mitigation and not enough on adaptation. In your answer you should:
• describe one mitigation strategy and one adaptation strategy
• explain advantages of each
• explain limitations of each
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained, well-evidenced evaluation. Names mitigation (Net Zero, offshore wind, 2030 EV ban) and adaptation (Pickering, Medmerry, urban tree planting) examples, develops advantages and limitations of each, reaches a justified judgement.
Secure (5–6): Clear evaluation. Two named strategies, advantages and drawbacks; conclusion present but partially justified.
Developing (3–4): Some evaluation. Strategies named in general terms; mostly one-sided; no clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2): Simple description of one strategy. No evaluation.
Indicative content: Mitigation tackles the cause (cuts CO2) but takes decades to bite. Adaptation copes with impacts already happening but does nothing to slow further change. Conclusion may say both are essential and that UK currently spends more on mitigation policy, while adaptation budgets struggle to keep up with rising flood risk.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the 'Sandford Principle' for UK National Parks?
options: Tourism comes first when conflicts arise
Conservation takes priority when there is a genuine conflict
Hill farmers have first call on land use
All decisions are voted on by local councils
